The Barred warbler (Curruca nisoria) is a relatively large sylviid that exhibits an interesting set of life-history trade-offs, particularly in its early development. Incubation, which occurs at a mean temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], is a critical period, and hatching typically takes place after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This incubation period is notably prolonged compared to smaller congeners, likely due to the greater thermal inertia of its eggs. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet body mass recorded at just 2.63 grams [Ww0 = 2.63 grams]. This precarious starting point demands intensive brooding, as the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental heat for thermoregulation during their first days of life.

Subsequent growth under the warmer conditions of the active metabolic period, typically around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], proceeds rapidly but follows a clear developmental schedule. The time until fledging, or the age at which the chick achieves its first flight, is documented as 11.5 days after hatching [tx = 11.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling phase is characteristic of many open-cup nesting passerines that face high predation pressure. Following this, the fledglings remain dependent on their parents for provisioning, but the onset of puberty marks a significant physiological transition. This species reaches sexual maturation at 34 days after hatching [tp = 34 days after hatching], a remarkably swift pace that allows individuals born early in the season to potentially breed the same summer at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

The robust adult body size of the Barred warbler supports a relatively high maximum reproductive output for a bird of its family. Females, which typically attain a maximum adult body mass of 26.3 grams [Wwi = 26.3 grams], consistently produce between 3 and 7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 7 eggs per clutch] during each breeding attempt. While males are slightly more diminutive, reaching a maximum recorded adult weight of 22.8 grams [Wwi = 22.8 grams], they are equally critical to the reproductive effort, providing substantial parental care. This sexual size dimorphism is modest but consistent across populations and is likely linked to the demands of territory defense, rather than any lekking or polygynous mating system.

Reproductive frequency in this species is heavily dictated by the length of the temperate breeding season. In their typical habitat, a breeding pair will raise between 1 and 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = between 1 and 2 clutches each year], a pattern that maximizes their annual output without placing excessive strain on the parents. The first reproductive event of a female's life, measured as the time since birth at first brood, generally occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This timing means that a bird hatched in early summer will overwinter as a juvenile and begin its first breeding attempt the following spring, a full year later. This obligatory waiting period underscores the importance of their long-distance migration in shaping their annual cycle.

The physiological underpinnings of this fast-paced life history are reflected in the species' energetic demands. Basal metabolic measurements, taken during the thermoneutral zone at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], show a maximal resting oxygen consumption of 69 milliliters per hour [JOi = 69 milliliters per hour]. This relatively high metabolic rate fuels both their active foraging lifestyle and the substantial energy required to feed a brood. Despite this high energy throughput, the maximum recorded longevity for the Barred warbler at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], a lifespan that is impressive for a bird of its mass and which allows for multiple seasons of reproductive experience, likely improving fledgling success rates with age.
